title: Sit in the dust of the wise (Avot 1:4)
hookLine: let your house be a meeting place for the wise; drink their words with thirst

cards: Two people are learning to fix a car. One watches a repair video at double speed while answering email.
The other spends a Saturday in a neighbor's garage, grease on his sleeves, handing over wrenches, asking why, getting told to be quiet and watch. Both are learning. Only one of them is getting dirty.
That kind of learning means getting close, being the least important person in the room, and wanting it badly. An old sage put all of that into one dusty picture.

teach.b: After Antigonus, Avot's chain passes to pairs of teachers. The first pair: Yose ben Yoezer and Yose ben Yochanan. Yose ben Yoezer says three things, in paraphrase.
Let your house be a meeting place for the wise.

teach.h: AT THEIR FEET, OR ON THEIR ROAD.
teach.b: Sit in the dust of their feet. And drink in their words with thirst. Start with the house.
Not the synagogue, not the school. Your house: a kitchen table where wise people want to come and talk. Then the dust.
The commentators give two pictures. In the old academies, students sat on the ground while the teacher sat above them, so you'd literally be in the dust at their feet.

Or students walked behind their teacher on dirt roads, close enough to catch every word, covered in the dust his feet kicked up. Either way: humble, close, and a bit dirty. Some readers hear more in the verb.
Mitabek comes from avak, dust. When Jacob wrestles a stranger through the night, the Torah's verb is vaye'avek, and Rashi explains it by the dust the two of them kicked up.
So for these readers, sitting in the dust of the wise can mean wrestling with them. Asking hard questions. Pushing back.
Last, drink their words with thirst.
Not polite sipping: the way you drink after a long run, gulping, grateful. Wisdom goes in best when you really want it.

how: Some Jews host study sessions and invite teachers into their homes, and traditional learning happens in pairs or small circles close to a teacher, arguing as well as listening.

o: getting close to the wise, sitting in their dust
staying humble by never questioning a teacher
cleaning a teacher's house as a sign of respect

games.q: three pieces of advice — tap the pairs.
p: a meeting place for the wise

s: Yose ben Yoezer says to invite the wise into your home
let your house be a meeting place for the wise.
sitting in the dust means staying silent and still
some readers link the verb to Jacob's wrestling in the dust; it can mean arguing and asking too.
students in the old academies sometimes sat on the ground before their teachers
that's one picture commentators give for sitting in the dust of their feet.

games.q: a wise teacher is passing through your town. what does Yose ben Yoezer say to do?
o: open your house, sit close, and drink in their words.
games.why: let your house be a meeting place for the wise, sit in the dust of their feet, and drink their words with thirst.

practice: Think of an older person who knows something you don't: a grandparent, a neighbor, a senior colleague, the old man at the hardware store. What could they teach you, a recipe, a trade, a story, how they got through a hard year?
Picture sitting near them, asking, and really listening, thirsty.

wordCard.voice: Mitabek. Sit, or wrestle, in the dust: the verb behind Yose ben Yoezer's saying to get close to the wise and drink in their words with thirst.

orig.note: Hebrew: sit, or wrestle, in the dust of their feet (Avot 1:4).

carryVoice: Your line: sit in the dust. A house that welcomes, a student who gets close, and real thirst. Day two hundred thirty-seven, done.
